en: Itivuttaka 76 Tikanipāta, Third Chapter Thus it was said by the Blessed One; thus has it been heard by me: “Monks, there are these three kinds of persons found existing in the world. What three? The person who is like a stone pillar, the person who is like a tree stump, and the person who is like a lotus flower. And how, monks, is one a person like a stone pillar? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with a mind full of hatred, harboring ill will toward beings. This, monks, is called a person like a stone pillar. And how, monks, is one a person like a tree stump? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with a mind devoid of hatred, free from ill will toward beings. However, he does not cultivate the path for the sake of attaining the unsurpassed security from bondage, nor does he apply himself to that end. This, monks, is called a person like a tree stump. And how, monks, is one a person like a lotus flower? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with a mind devoid of hatred, free from ill will toward beings. Furthermore, he cultivates the path for the sake of attaining the unsurpassed security from bondage and applies himself to that end. This, monks, is called a person like a lotus flower. These, monks, are the three kinds of persons found existing in the world. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Having said this, the Well-Farer, the Teacher, further said this: “The person like a stone pillar, And the person like a tree stump— But the person like a lotus flower, That one is truly called a sage. Thus was it said by the Blessed One, so I have heard.
The Discourse on the Foundation of Happiness.
This was said by the Blessed One, said by the Arahant; thus have I heard:
“Monks, desiring these three kinds of happiness, a wise person should guard their virtue.”
Which three?
A wise person should guard their virtue thinking, "May praise come to me"; a wise person should guard their virtue thinking, "May wealth arise for me";
a wise person should guard their virtue thinking, "With the breakup of the body, after death, may I be reborn in a happy destination, in a heavenly world."
“Monks, desiring these three kinds of happiness, a wise person should guard their virtue.
Thus the Blessed One spoke. With regard to this, it is said:
“A wise person, aspiring after three kinds of happiness— praise, the acquisition of wealth, and [the happiness of heaven]— should guard their virtue.”
And rejoicing in heaven after passing away.
Even if one does not commit evil oneself,
if one associates with one who commits it;
One becomes suspicious of evil,
and disrepute grows for them.
Whatever kind of friend one makes, [such is their own nature].
Whatever kind of person one associates with,
one indeed becomes like that;
for such is the nature of living together.
Serving one who serves,
or being touched by one who touches another—
like an arrow smeared with poison hitting a bundle of reeds—
What is unstained clings to it;
out of fear of such defilement, the wise person should never have evil friends.
The man who carries a putrid fish on the tip of a blade of kusa grass—
both the kusa grass and the fish give off a foul stench.
Such is the association with fools.
It is like a man who burns tagara incense with leaves.
Even the leaves waft a fragrant scent;
such is the association with the wise. Therefore, like a leaf-basket, [one should associate with the virtuous].
Having understood his own ripening,
the wise person should not associate with the unvirtuous, but should associate with the virtuous.
"The unwholesome lead to hell;
the wholesome cause one to reach a happy destination.
This matter was also spoken by the Blessed One; thus have I heard.
The seventh.
